A Semantic Image Search Engine

Retrieval examples and failure cases of machine reading of a personal photography collection.

Abstract

This project builds a semantic image search engine over a personal photography archive of 72 images. Using CLIP, each image is embedded once into a 512-dimensional vector space that is shared with natural language. At query time, a text prompt is embedded into the same space and cosine similarity is computed against every image embedding, returning the top-k most similar images in a Gradio interface. No captioning or text generation is involved.

The central finding is that CLIP's retrieval quality on personal photography is meaningfully lower than on internet imagery. This gap is structured by the mismatch between CLIP's training distribution (captioned web images) and the visual characteristics of personal archives (unconventional angles, personal context, absence of stock-photo composition). Documenting and mechanistically explaining this mismatch is the core contribution of this paper.

Motivation & Corpus Statement

Why this collection

I chose the pictures from my personal photography library from the past years because I know it intimately. I can immediately tell when the model retrieves something wrong.

What the collection contains

The 72 images contain mostly outdoor scenes, animals, architecture, and landscape. They were taken across different lighting conditions and times of day.

How it was curated

I selected images that covered a variety of visual categories to stress-test retrieval across scene types.

A note on rights: All images in this corpus are my own photography. No third-party copyrighted material is included.

Approach

The pipeline has four stages: image loading, embedding, indexing, and retrieval. CLIP is used as a joint text–image embedding model — both modalities are projected into the same 512-dimensional space, making direct comparison possible without any intermediate captioning or generation step.

Model choice

I used openai/clip-vit-base-patch32 — the smallest standard CLIP checkpoint. This divides each image into non-overlapping 32×32 pixel patches which are processed by a Vision Transformer (ViT). A larger model (clip-vit-large-patch14) uses finer 14×14 patches and produces better representations, but the base model is sufficient to demonstrate the pipeline and produces more interesting failure cases for analysis.

Retrieval Atlas

Ten documented queries — a mix of successes, partial matches, and failures. Each entry includes the query, the similarity threshold, the images returned, and a brief explanation grounded in embedding-space reasoning.

Search Query / Similarity Threshold0.19
Motorcycle
Blue motorcycle in front of a stone building
Blue motorcycle in front of a stone building with green windows

Even as the prompt became progressively more specific, the results did not narrow significantly because the similarity threshold was set too low. At 0.19, CLIP returns any image that weakly matches the query direction in embedding space, so increasing prompt specificity had limited effect — the threshold, not the query, was the binding constraint.





Search Query / Similarity Threshold0.190.22
Vehicle
Car

With the "car" prompt, CLIP returned images of mountains and trees despite the absence of any vehicle, likely because these backgrounds are common in commercial car photography in its training data. It also returned an image with a dog in the foreground, having detected the rear of a car in the background. With the "vehicle" prompt, a bicycle was returned as the top result — a semantically valid but unexpected interpretation, suggesting CLIP's embedding for "vehicle" skews towards lighter, more visually distinctive forms in this corpus.





Search Query / Similarity Threshold0.220.23
Picture of a man

CLIP correctly returned images containing human figures at lower thresholds, but also surfaced images of animals and sculptures. This suggests the model's representation of "man" is shaped by visual features such as upright posture and bilateral symmetry — features shared with certain animal poses and figurative sculpture — rather than semantic identity alone.





Search Query / Similarity Threshold0.24
Picture of a man. No animals and sculptures

The negative prompt had no effect on retrieval. CLIP operates through embedding similarity rather than instruction following — it has no mechanism to exclude concepts. A phrase like "no sculptures" is processed as part of the overall text embedding, and words like "sculptures" may actually pull the query vector closer to sculpture-related images rather than further away.





Search Query / Similarity Threshold0.240.260.27
Picture of a man by the sea

CLIP returned an image of a bird silhouette as the second highest-scoring result. This is likely because the image lacks clear facial features or distinguishing anatomy — the dark vertical silhouette with two legs is visually ambiguous enough to pattern-match to a standing human figure against a bright background, particularly in CLIP's patch-based representation.





Search Query / Similarity Threshold0.250.26
Picture of a kid by the sea

Following the previous experiment, I tested whether the same bird silhouette would score higher against a "kid" prompt given its proportions. At threshold 0.26 — identical to where it appeared as the second result for "man by the sea" — the bird image was the sole result returned. This suggests the silhouette's proportions align more closely with CLIP's embedding for a child's figure than an adult's.





Search Query / Similarity Threshold0.280.32
Red door
Red door frame of a building

Making the prompt more specific with "Red door frame of a building" improved precision at higher thresholds. The third result for the first prompt was a brown door adorned with red flowers, suggesting the model was influenced by the colour red and the door shape independently, without requiring both features to co-occur as a single object.





Search Query / Similarity Threshold0.220.230.24
Beach by the ocean
Sand beach by the ocean

Adding the single word "sand" to the prompt produced a notably different set of results. The more grounded, textural descriptor anchored the query embedding closer to actual beach imagery, whereas "beach by the ocean" alone retrieved results influenced by the broader semantic field of water and open space.





Search Query / Similarity Threshold0.160.21
Orange and brown butterfly with two antennas standing still on a blue curtain with a white wall on the background

At threshold 0.16, CLIP returned irrelevant images despite the high specificity of the prompt, demonstrating that a low threshold overrides prompt precision. At 0.21, the correct image was returned — suggesting the detailed description successfully directed the query vector, but only once the threshold was raised enough to filter out weaker matches.





Search Query / Similarity Threshold0.200.230.24
Cat
Search Query / Similarity Threshold0.200.24
Dog

For the "cat" prompt, CLIP returned images of a deer and doors before surfacing a dog. For "dog", images of cats appeared before the deer and doors. The cross-retrieval between cat and dog likely reflects shared contextual features — the cat images that scored for "dog" were outdoor photographs, an environment CLIP associates more strongly with dogs than indoor settings. This suggests the model is partially retrieving on scene context rather than the primary subject.





Limitations

LimitationWhy it happens
Negative prompts have no effectCLIP has no exclusion mechanism — all words contribute positively to the embedding direction
Scene context overrides subjectCLIP embeddings encode whole-image context, not isolated objects
